Description: Medical care CPI up 3.2% YoY in December 2025 (vs 2.9% in November). Medical care services index +3.5%, commodities +1.5%. Since 2000, medical care prices up 121.3% vs 86.1% general inflation.

However, employers report actual costs rising 7-9% due to utilization and demand factors not captured in CPI. The gap between CPI and employer experience suggests CPI understates true burden.
Data Quote: Medical CPI 3.2% YoY; services 3.5%; 121.3% cumulative since 2000 vs 86.1% general
Source: BLS CPI Dec 2025
Thesis Impact: CONSISTENT — costs still exceed general inflation but moderating
CARL Relevance: Premium burden affects discretionary spending

Notes: Employers projecting 9% increase for 2026

Description: KFF 2025 Survey: Average deductible $1,886 (single), up 17% since 2020 and 43% over decade. Small firms: $2,631 avg deductible; 53% face $2,000+. 34% of all workers in plans with $2,000+ deductible. 72% face OOP max >$3,000.
Analysis: CONSISTENT WITH THESIS. Deductible burden continues rising — $1,886 average is above ELEVATED threshold. Small firm workers particularly stressed (53% face $2,000+). The 17% 5-year increase outpaces wage growth. OOP maximums approaching ACA limits ($9,450 individual). This creates "functionally underinsured" population.
Data Quote: Avg deductible $1,886 (+17% 5yr, +43% 10yr); small firms $2,631; 53% small firm workers $2,000+
Source: KFF 2025 Employer Health Benefits Survey
Thesis Impact: CONSISTENT — validates OOP burden thesis
CARL Relevance: High deductibles create barrier to care; force credit use
Invalidation Criteria: If avg deductible declines or grows slower than wages
Notes: Family premium now $26,993

Description: Commonwealth Fund 2024 survey: 23% of insured Americans are underinsured (high OOP costs relative to income). 57% of underinsured forgo needed care due to cost. 66% of underinsured have employer coverage.
Analysis: CRITICAL FINDING. Nearly 1 in 4 insured adults are underinsured — insurance card doesn't mean access. Majority (66%) have employer coverage, contradicting assumption that employer plans are adequate. 57% forgoing care means underinsurance is not just financial — it's creating health consequences. This validates DOC thesis on coverage inadequacy.
Data Quote: 23% underinsured; 57% forgo care; 66% have employer coverage
Source: Commonwealth Fund 2024 Biennial Survey
Thesis Impact: CONSISTENT — underinsurance is widespread even with employer coverage
CARL Relevance: Underinsurance = latent medical debt risk
Invalidation Criteria: If underinsured rate declines below 20%
Notes: Definition: OOP >10% of income OR deductible >5% of income

Description: CFPB: $88B medical debt in collections affecting 20% of Americans (1 in 5). 4.1% have medical debt on credit reports (9.7M consumers, down from 27M in 2022 due to credit bureau policy changes). KFF broader definition: 41% have medical/dental debt.
Analysis: CONSISTENT WITH THESIS. Medical debt remains massive problem — $88B in collections. The apparent improvement (27M → 9.7M on credit reports) is largely due to credit bureau changes removing small debts and paid debts, not actual reduction in debt burden. KFF's 41% broader rate shows true prevalence. CFPB rule to remove medical debt was VACATED July 2025.
Data Quote: $88B in collections; 20% affected; 4.1% on credit reports (down from 27M to 9.7M); 41% broader definition
Source: CFPB, KFF
Thesis Impact: CONSISTENT — medical debt remains widespread; policy protection removed
CARL Relevance: Medical debt damages credit scores
Invalidation Criteria: If medical debt in collections declines materially
Notes: CFPB rule vacated July 2025

The 11% unable to access is alarming for developed nation.

Source: KFF, Gallup/West Health 2025

CARL Relevance: Deferred care → worse health → higher eventual costs

Insulin, cardiovascular, and mental health meds are highest risk categories.

Thesis Impact: CONSISTENT — medication non-adherence is widespread and deadly
CARL Relevance: Non-adherence leads to hospitalizations → medical debt
Invalidation Criteria: If non-adherence rate drops below 15%
Notes: Insulin rationing has caused deaths

However: (1) Only affects Medicare, not commercial; (2) Only 10 drugs initially; (3) Full savings take years to realize. This is partial thesis challenge for Rx segment but not invalidation.

CARL Relevance: Reduces Rx burden for Medicare population only
Invalidation Criteria: If IRA provisions repealed or scope dramatically expanded

Description: ACA marketplace enrollment closed at 23.1M for 2026 — down 1.2M (-4.9%) from 2025 record of 24.3M. Enhanced subsidies expired Dec 31, 2025. March 2026 survey: 9% of prior ACA enrollees now uninsured. Avg subsidized enrollee premiums up 114%. Urban Institute: 4.8M total coverage loss in 2026.
Analysis: ACUTE 2026 TRIGGER. This is the single most important new development since Session 1. ACA subsidy lapse is creating a new wave of uninsured at exactly the moment CARL's other stress vectors are elevated. More than half of those who reenrolled are cutting food/food spending to afford premiums. Self-employed, gig workers, early retirees (55-64) disproportionately affected.
Data Quote: 23.1M enrolled 2026 (-4.9%); 9% of prior enrollees uninsured; premiums +114% avg; 4.8M projected uninsured [Urban Inst]
Source: CMS 2026 OEP; CNBC Mar 19 2026; KFF Jan 2026; Urban Institute
Thesis Impact: CONSISTENT — new acute trigger for care deferral and medical debt accumulation
CARL Relevance: ACA uninsured = zero coverage = deferred care → eventual acute medical debt event. Overlaps with CARL's consumer spending stress (cutting food to pay premiums).
Invalidation Criteria: If Congress reinstates enhanced subsidies retroactively
Notes: 67% of public says Congress did "wrong thing" not extending (KFF) — political motivation for reinstatement exists

Description: GLP-1 drug cost shock crystallizing for employers in 2025-2026. Employer GLP-1 costs up ~30%. 64% of large employers say "significant" impact on Rx spending. GLP-1 claims rose from 6.9% to 10.5% of total Rx claims (2023-2025). Employers project 11-12% Rx cost trend 2026. 1-in-5 large firms (200+ workers) now cover GLP-1 for weight loss; 43% of firms with 5,000+ workers.
Analysis: STRUCTURAL ESCALATION. GLP-1 is now the dominant driver of Rx cost trend. Universal coverage could push premiums 14% higher. Coverage decisions are creating new within-workforce access gaps (top earners at large firms get GLP-1 coverage; small firm workers and self-employed do not). Self-pay cost $349-499/mo is not accessible for bottom 60%. This is a new K-shape driver within healthcare itself.
Data Quote: GLP-1 employer costs +30%; claims 6.9%→10.5%; 64% large employers "significant"; 43% of 5,000+ firms covering
Source: KFF EHBS 2025; Mercer GLP-1 2026; PwC Behind the Numbers 2026
Thesis Impact: CONSISTENT — reinforces cost driver thesis; new K-shape within healthcare
CARL Relevance: GLP-1 costs pass through to all worker premiums even for those who don't use them; creates new healthcare cost wedge
Invalidation Criteria: If biosimilar competition drives GLP-1 prices below $100/mo (not before ~2032)
Notes: GLP-1 without competition until 2032+; structural cost driver for the thesis window

Description: Rural hospital financial crisis deepening. 182 total closures since 2010 (18 in past year). 46% of rural hospitals have negative operating margins. 432 rural hospitals at risk of closure. Medicaid non-expansion states: 53% rural hospitals in red, median margin -1.5%. Labor and delivery closures accelerating: 116 closures since 2020, 27 in 2025 alone. ACA subsidy lapse costing rural hospitals est. $1.6B in patient revenue.
Analysis: STRUCTURAL ACCELERATION. Rural hospital access crisis is compounding consumer healthcare stress. Rural communities (disproportionately lower-income) lose access, forcing longer travel times, delayed care, or no care at all. L&D closure surge is particularly acute — 116 closures means pregnant women in rural areas traveling 50+ miles to deliver. Medicare sequestration cut costs rural hospitals $509M/yr. Policy headwinds from ACA lapse + potential Medicaid cuts are compounding already-stressed margins.
Data Quote: 182 closures since 2010; 46% negative margin; 432 at risk; 116 L&D closures since 2020
Source: Chartis 2025 State of Rural Health; Fierce Healthcare; Commonwealth Fund Feb 2026
Thesis Impact: CONSISTENT — access crisis is structural; accelerating K-shape geography
CARL Relevance: Rural communities = disproportionately bottom 60% — this is access desert formation
Invalidation Criteria: If Rural Hospital Closure Relief Act (S.502) passes with meaningful funding
Notes: S.502 introduced but passage uncertain; Medicaid expansion in holdout states would help most

Source: KFF Health Tracking Poll Jan 2026 (conducted Jan 13-20, 2026, n=1,426)

Description: Medicare GLP-1 Bridge Program: CMS announced temporary program July 1 - Dec 31, 2026. Covers Wegovy, Zepbound, Foundayo for weight loss via Part D plans at flat $50/mo copay (outside Part D benefit — does not count toward $2,100 OOP cap or deductible). LIS enrollees do NOT get LIS subsidy applied. BALANCE Model launches Medicare Part D GLP-1 coverage Jan 1, 2027. Medicaid BALANCE model: May 2026 for opt-in states. Employer coverage: 49% of 500+ employee plans covering weight-loss GLP-1 (up from ~43% prior data point per Mercer 2025).
Analysis: SIGNIFICANT NEW DEVELOPMENT. Medicare GLP-1 Bridge is a policy signal that Washington is moving to cover weight-loss GLP-1s eventually (BALANCE Model in 2027). The $50 copay is meaningful for Medicare population. However: (1) $50 copay outside Part D = no OOP cap credit; (2) LIS exclusion means lowest-income Medicare patients don't get best deal; (3) Still creates access gap vs. commercial employer plans that cover at $0-$50 tiered. For employer side: 49% of large firm coverage (up from 43%) continues to drive K-shape within employment — large-employer workers get access, small-firm workers and self-employed do not.
Data Quote: Medicare GLP-1 Bridge: $50/mo copay, Jul-Dec 2026; Wegovy/Zepbound covered; outside Part D benefit; BALANCE Model Jan 2027; employer coverage 49% of 500+ firms
Source: CMS Medicare GLP-1 Bridge program; KFF Quick Take; Mercer National Survey of Employer-Sponsored Health Plans 2025; AARP 2026 Medicare coverage guide
Thesis Impact: CONSISTENT — GLP-1 access gap between Medicare/Medicaid and commercial persists; K-shape within access continues
CARL Relevance: GLP-1 cost shock still loading on employer plans; partial Medicare relief but with access cliff for LIS enrollees
POLLY Link: POLLY (Medicare Advantage cost trend from GLP-1 adoption)
Invalidation Criteria: If biosimilar competition drives GLP-1 prices below $100/mo (not before ~2032)
Notes: BALANCE Model in 2027 is the more permanent Medicare solution; Bridge is 6-month stopgap

Description: Q1 2026 hospital financial picture: Kaufman Hall "new normal" report (Feb 10, 2026 release): 2025 YTD adjusted operating margin 1.3%; bad debt and charity care rising; revenue shifting from private to public payers; provider productivity (wRVUs) up 7% since 2023 but reimbursement per wRVU DOWN 1%; median physician practice subsidy $315K Q4 2025; labor costs 84.4% of expenses. Key signals: (1) 734 hospitals at risk (CHQPR) vs 432 prior Chartis figure — risk universe expanding; (2) distressed M&A at record 43.5% = financially fragile facilities being absorbed or failing; (3) physician practice subsidies rising ($315K) = hospitals cross-subsidizing practices to maintain volumes; (4) reimbursement per wRVU falling = physicians doing more for less, workforce pressure building. All consistent with DOC-P04 (200 closures total by end 2026).

Source: Kaufman Hall National Hospital Flash Report Feb 10, 2026; Becker's Hospital Review Apr 2026; CHQPR 2026 at-risk analysis; Chief Healthcare Executive Jan 2026

Invalidation Criteria: If Medicaid expansion in holdout states + Rural Hospital Closure Relief Act passes with material funding
Notes: S.502 (Rural Hospital Closure Relief Act) introduced but passage uncertain; budget headwinds in 2026

Description: CFPB 2026 enforcement posture update: In 2025-2026 CFPB dismissed 6 FCRA/Regulation V enforcement actions following administration change. No new medical debt regulatory requirements expected in 2026. CFPB medical debt rule (Jan 2025) was vacated Jul 11, 2025 by Texas court. State-level laws: 15 states with own reporting protections (unchanged). Medical debt collection agencies operating under reduced federal scrutiny — compliance burdens easing.
Analysis: CONSISTENT — WORSENING DIRECTION. CFPB neutering means the only brake on medical debt damage to credit reports is now state laws (15 states). 35 states have no medical debt credit reporting protection. For the 65% of Americans in unprotected states: medical bills that go to collections WILL appear on credit reports and damage credit scores. This removes a key mitigation mechanism and is thesis-amplifying. With ACA uninsured surge loading in 2026, the pipeline from coverage loss → acute care event → medical debt → credit report damage is now unrestricted at federal level.
Data Quote: CFPB dismissed 6 enforcement actions 2025-2026; no new 2026 medical debt rules; state laws: 15 states with protection; federal rule vacated Jul 2025
Source: Healpay CFPB analysis 2026; GovPing/Changeflow CFPB enforcement landscape Apr 1, 2026; CFPB newsroom
Thesis Impact: CONSISTENT — removes consumer protection; thesis-amplifying for medical debt → credit damage channel
CARL Relevance: Medical debt → credit score damage → reduced credit access → CARL's credit deterioration vectors; CFPB enforcement vacuum amplifies this
Invalidation Criteria: If CFPB reinstates enforcement posture or Congress passes medical debt legislation
Notes: 15 state laws are patchwork; most medical debt held by consumers in unprotected states

Description: Medical care CPI YoY: Aug 2026 1.6% (MoM -0.2%), Sep 2026 1.5% (MoM +0.1%). Services 2.5% both months; commodities -2.7% Aug, -3.3% Sep; hospital services 12-mo +5.2% (Aug), MoM +0.7% (Sep). All-items 3.4% Aug / 3.7% Sep; core 2.4% / 2.6%. July medical-care YoY not obtained.
Analysis: Headline medical CPI is now BELOW all-items CPI and is falling because drug prices are falling (commodities -3.3%), not because care is getting cheaper: hospital services run +5.2% YoY. Composition, not relief. DOC-P03 (>4% in 2026) is effectively dead.
Data Quote: Medical care 1.5% Sep / 1.6% Aug; services 2.5%; commodities -3.3% / -2.7%; hospital services +5.2% (Aug 12-mo)
Source: BLS CPI releases 2026-09-11 (Aug) and 2026-10-14 (Sep), bls.gov
Thesis Impact: WEAKENS headline-CPI channel; hospital-services leg intact
CARL Relevance: Medical CPI below headline CPI = relative-price relief at the commodity level only
Invalidation Criteria: ML-DOC-02 invalidation (medical CPI below general CPI 2+ quarters) is now in play: Sep 1.5 vs 3.7, Aug 1.6 vs 3.4; check whether Jul and Jun also sat below headline before calling it
Notes: Next CPI Tue 2026-11-10 (Oct). Single-month rule: do not read Sep +0.7% hospital MoM as a trend.

Description: KFF 2026 Employer Health Benefits Survey (rel 2026-10-22): family premium $28,303 (+5%), single $9,804 (+5%); worker family contribution $7,471 (+9%, +$621); single deductible $1,955 (similar to 2025), small firms $2,624, large $1,772. GLP-1 for weight loss covered by 18% of 200+ firms (19% in 2025); 16% at 200-999; 12% of non-covering firms stopped in past 12 months. Mercer/Marsh prelim (Sep 2026): 2027 cost per employee +8.2% after actions (11% with no action), biggest since 2003; BGH 2027 +9.2%, pharmacy +12%; Aon 2027 +9.5%.
Analysis: Employer-side premium growth printed 5%, half of DOC-P02's 9-11% band: P02 MISSED. The squeeze is being passed to workers (contribution +9% vs wages +3.7%) and pushed into 2027 (8-9.5% projections). Top-40% channel is real but runs through paycheck deductions, not deductibles (deductible flat).
Data Quote: Family premium $28,303 +5%; worker share $7,471 +9%; 2027 Mercer +8.2%
Source: KFF EHBS 2026 kff.org (2026-10-22); Mercer/Marsh newsroom Sep 2026; Business Group on Health Aug 2026; Aon Aug 2026
Thesis Impact: MIXED: magnitude miss for 2026, cost shift to worker accelerating
CARL Relevance: Worker premium contribution +9% vs wages +3.7% = take-home squeeze
POLLY Link: POLLY premium/plan-design side owns premium detail
Invalidation Criteria: 2027 final Mercer survey (year-end) prints below 6.7%
Notes: Mercer 2027 figures are preliminary (responses through Aug 10).

Description: Census CPS-ASEC (rel Sep 2026): 2025 full-year uninsured 26.7M = 7.9% (2024: 27.1M, 8.0%; not statistically different). CDC NHIS 2025 point-in-time 8.3%. Commonwealth Fund 2026 Biennial (field May-Jul 2026, published 2026-10-22): uninsured age 19-64 11.2% (2024: 8.9%); underinsured 23% (unchanged); 46% inadequately insured; 50% delayed/avoided care for cost (46% in 2022). CMS: effectuated ACA enrollment Feb-2026 19.17M vs 21.78M Feb-2025 (-12%).
Analysis: The 2025 Census print is a pre-cliff baseline and says nothing about 2026. The first 2026-vintage measurement (Commonwealth, survey) shows working-age uninsured +2.3pp in two years: the ACA cliff showing up in coverage data. Survey, not administrative; Census 2026 lands Sep 2027.
Source: Census P60-291 (Sep 2026); AHA News 2026-10-23 and AJMC/Becker's 2026-10-22 on Commonwealth Fund; CBPP reproducing CMS effectuated table
Thesis Impact: CONSISTENT — ACA cliff visible in first 2026-vintage coverage measurement
CARL Relevance: New uninsured cohort = deferred medical debt loader for 2027
Invalidation Criteria: Census 2026 (Sep 2027) shows uninsured not statistically higher
Notes: Commonwealth figures read through AHA/AJMC/Becker's, not the primary PDF — verify at commonwealthfund.org before formal citation.

Description: KFF 'Americans' Challenges with Health Care Costs' (updated 2026-10-23): 28% of adults skipped/postponed needed care due to cost in past 12 months (KFF Survey of Health Access and Caregiving, May 4-26 2026); 62% of uninsured under-65; 15% say health got worse; 22% problems paying medical bills; 62% worried about affording care (Sep 16-21 2026 poll); 43% cost-related Rx behavior (Feb-Mar 2026, up from 33% 2025). Page states the 36% figure applies to adults 18-64 with 3+ chronic conditions. West Health-Gallup: 2025 annual (Jun-Aug 2025 field) ~1 in 3 skipped; 2026 annual not yet published.
Analysis: DOC's dashboard 36% care-deferral figure is not a 2026 print. It traces to KFF's May-2025 Tracking Poll and was carried as 'KFF Jan/Apr 2026 reprint'. The 2026 KFF figure is 28%, from a different survey instrument, so 36 to 28 is not a measured decline. Either way neither instrument is near 40%: DOC-P05 MISSED.
Data Quote: 28% skipped/postponed care (May 2026); 62% uninsured
Source: KFF kff.org/health-costs/americans-challenges-with-health-care-costs (2026-10-23)
Thesis Impact: WEAKENS the 'approaching 40%' framing; uninsured 62% intact
CARL Relevance: Deferral concentrated in uninsured (62%) = ACA cliff cohort
Invalidation Criteria: Gallup-West Health 2026 annual prints >=38%
Notes: Instrument change (Tracking Poll to Survey of Health Access) means no like-for-like trend. Commonwealth 50% avoided care is a broader construct, not comparable.

Description: Hospital margins: Vizient/Kaufman Hall Flash August-2026 data (rel ~2026-10-13): nearly half of hospitals in the red (43% per Becker's); Becker's reports national margin index 1.8% Aug vs 3.8% Jul and 5.6% Jun, down 2pp YoY; bad debt + charity care +13% YoY; operating revenue/day +6%. Closures: Becker's 2026 counts full hospital/ED closures well below 2025 pace (3-6 YTD vs 13-21 same point 2025; 2025 full year 23); rural workforce reductions 15% of 68 cuts (vs <10% 2025); 41 service-line closures since Jul 1.
Analysis: Hospital distress is moving from closures into service-line cuts and bad debt. Bad debt + charity care +13% YoY is the hospital-side mirror of the patient-side medical-debt channel: the strongest system-stress signal this refresh.
Data Quote: Bad debt + charity care +13% YoY (Aug 2026); 43% hospitals in red
Source: Becker's Hospital Review roundups of Vizient/Kaufman Hall Aug-2026 flash; Becker's closure trackers Oct 2026
Thesis Impact: CONSISTENT — debt channel visible at provider level
CARL Relevance: Provider bad debt rising = consumer medical debt forming before it reaches bureaus
Invalidation Criteria: Bad debt growth falls below revenue growth for 2+ months
Notes: Margin figures are via Becker's, not the Vizient primary (page shows only headline takeaways). The Jun 5.6% / Jul 3.8% values need primary verification; KH monthly margins are volatile.

Description: CARL packet 2026-08-11 (HHDC Q2): share with a collection 4.60/4.98/4.88% (Q4-25/Q1-26/Q2-26); average collection per person $1,678/$1,540/$1,577. Bureau policy: paid medical collections and medical collections under $500 excluded since 2023 (voluntary, still in force; CFPB rule vacated 2025-07-11).
Analysis: Neither branch (composition vs severity) is established. The Q2 +2.4% average is a partial rebound of Q1's -8.2%; on net the Q2 average is -6.0% below Q4. The <$500 threshold has been fixed since 2023, so it cannot explain a quarter-on-quarter change by itself. Read: noise inside a range, not a medical-debt signal. Re-test on the Q3 HHDC (early Nov 2026) with 4+ quarters.
Source: CARL inbox packet 2026-08-11 (NY Fed HHDC Q2 2026); bureau 2022-23 medical-debt reporting commitments
Thesis Impact: NEUTRAL — no bureau-primary corroboration yet
CARL Relevance: HHDC collections bucket = candidate flow-side instrument for DOC-P06
Invalidation Criteria: Q3 HHDC average rises above $1,678 with share flat or up = severity branch
Notes: Answer to CARL KB-CARL-382 ask; packet was 78 days old when read.

Description: HCA Q3 2026 (8-K + call, 2026-10-27): uninsured ~10.5% of equivalent admissions vs 8.5% Q3-25; exchange equivalent admissions -19% YoY (+8% QoQ); ~80% of uninsured growth = exchange enrollees moving ~1-for-1 to uninsured, ~20% fewer Medicaid conversions (mostly Texas); ~$400M pre-tax hit in the quarter; same-facility ER visits +5.1%, inpatient surgeries -1.4%, outpatient surgeries -3.7%. UHS Q3 (2026-10-28): exchange volumes -17% with a similar rise in self-pay, <$25M impact. CHS Q3: revenue -10.7%, 'payor mix and acuity did not develop as expected'. Tenet Q2: exchange admissions -13.5%, 1-for-1 to uninsured.
Analysis: Administrative-grade confirmation of the ACA cliff: people who drop marketplace coverage keep showing up at the hospital, now uninsured. ER up, elective surgery down = care shifting from scheduled to emergency, which is the deferred-care pattern. This is where medical debt is being created right now; bureau data will lag.
Data Quote: Uninsured 10.5% of equivalent admissions vs 8.5%; exchange -19%; $400M Q3 hit
Source: HCA 8-K ex99.1 (sec.gov, 2026-10-27); HCA Q3 call transcript (fool.com 2026-10-27); UHS Q3 call (2026-10-28); CHS 8-K Q3
Thesis Impact: CONSISTENT — strongest administrative evidence of the cliff to date
CARL Relevance: Hospital self-pay surge = medical-debt origination before bureau reporting
Invalidation Criteria: HCA Q4 (Jan 2027) uninsured share back below 9%
Notes: 10.5%/8.5% and the 80/20 split are from the call transcript, not the 8-K; the $400M is in both. HCA guides that 2027 exchange losses will be smaller than 2026's.

Description: Urban Institute (rel 2026-10-06, Well-Being and Basic Needs Survey, Dec-2025 field, n>10,000): 26.6% of adults report family medical debt; 15% past-due or unable to pay; of those with debt 53.8% owe >=$1,000, 15.5% >=$5,000; hospitals the source for 52%; 26% of insured vs 35% of uninsured. Relief programs: Michigan $21M / 9,767 people (10/14); Massachusetts $38M / ~70,000 (10/26); Illinois >$1.4B / ~700,000 cumulative; Lexington KY ~$8M / 4,100.
Analysis: Survey prevalence is high and mostly insured people, but it is a Dec-2025 snapshot, before most of the cliff. Charity debt relief is now a measurable offset at state level (Illinois alone >$1.4B), which will dampen bureau-visible collections in those states: one more reason HHDC may under-read the channel.
Data Quote: 26.6% family medical debt; 52% owed to hospitals
Source: Urban Institute via Managed Healthcare Executive 2026-10-06, Becker's; state press releases (michigan.gov 2026-10-14, WBUR 2026-10-26, Capitol News Illinois)
Thesis Impact: CONSISTENT (prevalence); relief = measurement confounder
CARL Relevance: Debt relief programs suppress collections data
Notes: Urban 26.6% and KFF 41% (2022) use different definitions; do not trend them against each other.

Description: WTW Best Practices survey (rel 2026-10-28): 16% of employers covering GLP-1s for weight loss are considering dropping coverage (9% prior year); 8% steer workers to cash channels, 28% planning or considering it. CNBC 2026-10-27: employer plans dropping GLP-1 coverage for 2027. Novo ~50% Wegovy list-price cut effective 2027-01-01 (cash prices unchanged). Cash: Wegovy pill from $149, shot from $199; Zepbound from $299; orforglipron from $149. UNH Q3 (2026-10-13): commercial benefit trend >11%, driven by specialty drugs and No Surprises Act costs.
Analysis: The 2027 benefit-design retreat is broadening (WTW 9→16% considering a drop). Employers are moving GLP-1 users from coverage to cash: a cost shift onto employees that falling cash prices only partly offset. Commercial trend >11% at the largest insurer backs the 2027 +8-9.5% employer projections.
Data Quote: WTW 16% considering dropping (vs 9%); UNH commercial trend >11%
Source: WTW via 24/7 Wall St 2026-10-28; CNBC 2026-10-27; UNH Q3 call 2026-10-13 (fool.com)
Thesis Impact: CONSISTENT — cost shift to workers
CARL Relevance: GLP-1 coverage to cash = OOP shift for covered users
Notes: WTW figures via secondary coverage; P07 still carries its resolvability defect, this does not fix it.

Description: ACA 2027 OEP Nov 1 2026 to Jan 15 2027 (Dec 15 for Jan 1 coverage). Insurers' proposed 2027 median gross premium +15% (~10pts medical cost, ~4pts subsidy-expiry morbidity); final rates vary by state (NY ~6% approved vs ~20% requested). No enhanced-subsidy extension found in 2026. Medicaid work requirements: national start Jan 1 2027; Nebraska (May), Montana (Jul; grace period ended Oct 1, enrollees can now lose coverage), Iowa (Dec). Urban/RWJF: 5-10M lose Medicaid in 2028, 3-7M from work requirements; 25-state suit to block denied in July. HCA: ~15-20% of its expansion-state Medicaid patients subject to work requirements, 'modest' 2027 impact.
Analysis: Second year of the cliff starts Nov 1 at higher gross premiums. Montana is the first state where work-requirement disenrollment can now happen: first live test of DOC-P09's mechanism ahead of the Jan 1 national start.
Data Quote: 2027 proposed median +15%; Montana grace ended Oct 1
Source: CBPP OEP blog; healthinsurance.org; Urban/RWJF via Healthcare Dive; Stateline; HCA Q3 call
Thesis Impact: CONSISTENT
Notes: Enhanced-subsidy status: searches returned only 2025 coverage; 'no extension' is by absence of 2026 news, not a confirmed statement. P09 says 'Dec 31 2026'; national work-requirement start is Jan 1 2027 — same event.
